summary: Emil Kowalski argues that AI can write animation code but cannot tell what feels right, so it produces motion that works yet feels mediocre, and people who cannot tell the difference ship it. The page is a set of interactive exercises: each shows two animations side by side, the reader picks the better one, writes down why, then reads the author's breakdown. The exercises cover the size of the animated element, easing, entry animations, being intentional, frequency of use, using scale, removing elements, handling interruptions, popovers, stagger and layered motion. For a design system this suggests a review bar: motion is not done when it works, it is done when someone has compared alternatives and can name why one feels better [inferred]. The captured text contains the exercise prompts and demo labels only, not the author's verdicts or values.
key_ideas: AI can write animation code but cannot judge what feels right.
Motion that merely works but feels mediocre should not be shipped; good enough is not good enough.
Judgement is a trainable skill: spot what is wrong, name it, then fix it.
Training method: compare two animations side by side, pick one, write down why, then check an expert breakdown.
Putting into words why something feels right trains your ability to articulate judgement, which the author says will be incredibly valuable in the AI era.
The dimensions the author trains are: element size, easing, entry animations, intentionality, frequency of use, scale, removing elements, interruptions, popovers, stagger and layered motion.
Several exercises can only be judged by interacting with them: hovering through both lists, opening and closing each menu rapidly, and removing chips.
How often an element is used is part of judging its animation.
The author's design engineering skill file packages these rules so coding agents can follow them in practice.

rules.rule: Do not ship animation code, including AI-written code, just because it works; check that the motion feels right before shipping.
rules.why: AI produces motion that works but feels mediocre; if you cannot tell the difference you will ship it and settle for good enough, which is not good enough.
rules.evidence: opening: 'It produces motion that works, but feels mediocre'

rules.rule: When reviewing motion, spot what is wrong, name the problem in words, and then fix it.
rules.why: This is the ability the author says the exercises train.
rules.evidence: 'trains your ability to spot what’s wrong, name it, and fix it'

rules.rule: To train motion judgement, compare two animations side by side and pick the better one.
rules.why: This is the format of every exercise the author uses to train judgement.
rules.evidence: 'Each exercise shows two animations side by side'

rules.rule: Write down why you chose a variant before reading an expert breakdown, then compare your reasoning with it.
rules.why: Putting into words why something feels right trains your ability to articulate judgement, which the author calls incredibly valuable in the AI era.

rules.evidence: Handling interruptions: 'Open and close each menu rapidly'

rules.rule: Judge the hover animation of a frequently used list, such as an options menu, by hovering through the whole list and choosing what feels better for frequent use.
rules.why: Frequency of use is one of the author's judgement exercises; he asks which feels better for something you would use frequently.
rules.evidence: Frequency of use: 'Hover through both lists'

rules.rule: Take the size of the animated element into account when choosing its animation, for example a mobile menu.
rules.why: Size of an element is one of the author's judgement exercises; the preferred variant is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Size of an element: 'Which mobile menu animation feels better?'

rules.rule: Choose the easing for a toast animation deliberately, comparing variants and picking the one that feels better.
rules.why: Choosing the right easing is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on a toast; the preferred curve is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Choosing the right easing: 'Which toast animation feels better?'

rules.rule: Treat a dialog's entrance animation as its own decision and compare entrances before choosing one.
rules.why: Entry animations is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on an 'Open dialog' button; the preferred variant is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Entry animations: 'Click both buttons. Which entrance feels better?'

rules.rule: Be intentional about how an accordion animates when it opens and closes.
rules.why: Being intentional is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on an FAQ accordion; the preferred variant is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Being intentional: 'Which accordion animation feels better?'

rules.rule: Use scale deliberately in button press feedback, comparing press variants before choosing one.
rules.why: Using scale properly is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on a Subscribe button; the preferred scale is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Using scale properly: 'Which press feels better?'

rules.rule: Make removing elements, such as chips, feel smooth, and judge it by actually removing chips in both variants.
rules.why: Removing elements is one of the author's judgement exercises, and smoothness is the criterion he asks readers to judge by.
rules.evidence: Removing elements: 'Remove chips on both sides. Which feels smoother?'

rules.rule: Compare popover animation variants by clicking the trigger button before choosing how a popover animates.
rules.why: Animating popovers is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on a 'Show details' button; the preferred variant is not in the captured text.

rules.rule: When staggering a hero section's entrance, judge the stagger by whether the entrance feels intentional.
rules.why: Using stagger is one of the author's judgement exercises, and 'more intentional' is the criterion he asks readers to judge by.
rules.evidence: Using stagger: 'Which entrance feels more intentional?'

rules.rule: Consider layered motion when animating a side panel opening over a page such as a dashboard.
rules.why: Layered motion is one of the author's judgement exercises, shown on a side panel over a dashboard; the preferred variant is not in the captured text.
rules.evidence: Layered motion: 'Open the side panel on both'

process.detail: Build or find two versions of the same animation and place them side by side (the source provides the pairs; building your own is an adaptation) [inferred].
Use each the way the exercises ask: click the trigger, hover through the list, open and close the menu rapidly, or remove chips.
Choose the variant that feels better for the stated criterion, such as smoother, more intentional, better under interruption, or better for frequent use.
Put into words why the chosen variant feels right before looking at any expert opinion.
Read an expert breakdown and compare it with your reasoning.
In your own motion, spot what is wrong, name it and fix it; give coding agents the design engineering skill file so they follow the same rules.

caveats: The captured text holds only the exercise headings, prompts and demo labels. The interactive demos and the author's breakdowns (which variant is better, why, and any durations, curves or scale values) were not captured, so the per-exercise rules state the criterion and the test method only, not the preferred answer. A re-capture that includes the revealed breakdowns is needed to extract the actual values.
Because the verdicts are missing, rules marked 'consider' name a dimension to judge rather than a settled house standard.

The page opens with a plug for the author's course aiforui.dev (early access noted as closed) and ends with a plug for animations.dev, described as teaching practical animation techniques to make products feel cleaner, faster and more polished; both are self-promotion, not guidance.
The 'design engineering skill file' is referenced without a link in the captured text; that it is the emilkowalski/skills repository is an assumption [inferred].
The claim that articulating judgement will be incredibly valuable in the AI era is the author's opinion, not a measured finding.
